pr_title: Decoding PKCS#8: separate decoding of encrypted and unencrypted PKCS#8
pr_body:
This has us switch from the 'structure' "pkcs8" to "PrivateKeyInfo",
which is sensible considering we already have "SubjectPublicKeyInfo".
We also add "EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo", and use it for a special decoder
that detects and decrypts an EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structured DER
blob into a PrivateKeyInfo structured DER blob and passes that on to
the next decoder implementation.

The result of this change is that PKCS#8 decryption should only happen
once per decoding instead of once for every expected key type.
Furthermore, this new decoder implementation sets the data type to the
OID of the algorithmIdentifier field, thus reducing how many decoder
implementations are tentativaly run further down the call chain.

A profile build showed me one difference that I believe is crucial:

master:

```
Each sample counts as 0.01 seconds.
  %   cumulative   self              self     total           
 time   seconds   seconds    calls  us/call  us/call  name    
...
  0.00      0.30     0.00    37037     0.00     0.26  ossl_decoder_from_algorithm
```

this PR:

```
Each sample counts as 0.01 seconds.
  %   cumulative   self              self     total           
 time   seconds   seconds    calls  ms/call  ms/call  name    
...
```

This is due to `OSSL_DECODER_do_all_provided()` *re-creating* every decoder method, *every time it's called*, i.e. it doesn't do the "normal" pre-fetching.  There are technical reasons behind this, but I strongly believe that if we make that (oh, *all* XXX_do_all_provided()!) do the "normal" pre-fetching of methods, only the first run should take any noticable time.
A separate issue should be raised about this.

There may be some structural issues to address before doing that. This `collect_extra_decoder` function seems to called 2000 times in a *single* private key parsing operation.

Poking around the code in the profile, it seems OpenSSL is quadratic in the number of decoders you have, and there are quite a lot of them. I don't fully follow what `OSSL_DECODER_CTX_add_extra` is doing, but it seems OpenSSL now models generic "container" formats like PEM, PrivateKeyInfo, etc., as pluggable conversion functions with input/output formats? And then, before it does anything, it looks like `OSSL_DECODER_CTX_add_extra` tries to build all possible paths through these conversion functions, matching inputs to outputs?

That first layer of this path-building starts with a set of leaf "decoder instances" and then, for each one (twice, actually), iterates over every "decoder" to find the ones that can chain backwards to that decoder instances input type. That means decoders are tapped on the head 2 * decoder_instances * decoders times. (And then the next layer adds another O(decoders) iterations. I suspect this would also go exponential if the wrong series of container formats were added to the system.)

I couldn't find any documentation on why this path-builder design was chosen. It is a little odd to me because one shouldn't need to explore the whole tree of paths to parse one input. I think this comes out of OpenSSL working backwards from all possible outputs, rather than working forwards from the one input you have. The way these container formats are designed (and generally when parsing things), the forwards is the natural direction:

* Based on `PEM_read_PrivateKey` being called, we know the input is PEM. PEM is a type string (`BEGIN WHATEVER`) followed by base64-encoded data.
* Run the PEM decoder to get out the type string and base64-decode the data. This decoder can be key-independent. It's just fancy base64.
* Based on the type string, call the appropriate decoder on the data. This could be made pluggable by allowing providers to register decoders for PEM types
  * In @hannob's sample, the type is `RSA PRIVATE KEY`, so you find the provider(s) that support `RSA PRIVATE KEY` and ask them to parse the data. They should parse an RSAPrivateKey ASN.1 structure and that's the end of it.
  * In the original report, the type is `PRIVATE KEY`. That means the type is PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo. That too is a generic, provider-independent format that, more-or-less, expands to another (type, data) pair. This time the type is an AlgorithmIdentifier.
    * Call the PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo decoder to extract the type and data. This decoder can also be key-independent.
    * Now, based on the type OID in the PrivateKeyInfo, call the appropriate decoder. This likewise can be made pluggable by allowing providers to register decoders for PKCS#8 types.
    * If the type is rsaEncryption, find the provider(s) that support that and ask them to parse the data. They should again parse an RSAPrivateKey ASN.1 structure and that's the end of it.

At no point do you need to explore every possible chain of decoders. The only operation you need is "I have an input of format X. Call the function that parses X". Where there need only be a single implementation, that can be a direct function call. Where you wish it to be pluggable, that only needs a simple lookup. A container format decoder is just something that needs to do that dispatch a second time.

Now that 3.2 is released and you all are working on 3.3, I may suggest taking some time to think about the structural issues in the encoder/decoder system. Working backwards and guessing formats is not a performant, secure, or well-defined way to decode an input. Start from the input type that the caller asked you to parse and work forwards.

This is already on our radar of things we might get into 3.3:

https://github.com/openssl/project/issues/100

> Start from the input type that the caller asked you to parse and work forwards.

Unfortunately we will also have to support the wildcard decoding as regressing this is not an option.

> Unfortunately we will also have to support the wildcard decoding as regressing this is not an option.

By wildcard decoding, I assume you mean where the caller forgets to tell you the format, and OpenSSL has to try between several overlapping (i.e. ambiguous) formats? Ambiguous parsers are a thoroughly well-studied and well-understood source of [security](https://www.adambarth.com/papers/2009/barth-caballero-song.pdf) [vulnerabilities](https://www.brainonfire.net/blog/2022/04/11/what-is-parser-mismatch/), not to mention unpredictable behavior (i.e backwards compatibility risks). Hopefully you all carefully analyzed all pairs of supported formats before exposing them to be part of a wildcard decode. E.g. all 32-byte strings are valid raw X25519 keys, but a 32-byte string may also be something else entirely, so raw X25519 can never participate in such a scheme.

Design problems aside, I see no reason why it requires this backwards parse. Even if the caller forgets to tell you the format, that problem only applies at the top level. Once you've decided to try, say, DER PKCS#8 PrivateKeyInfo, or PEM[*], all parsing from then on is unambiguous. You only need to try ambiguous cases and backtrack at the top-level. And, of course, even if you did need to backtrack on the inner layers (again, you do not), that's still no reason to build the graph ahead of time.

You really don't need to pre-explore all possible call graphs like this. It's just overhead, not flexibility.

[*] PEM and DER are not analogous, so a good parser API design would take this into account. PEM contains a type header, so the caller can actually say "I have a PEM private key" and let the library dispatch between "BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY" and "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY". Whereas a DER encoding is not necessarily sufficient to identify the structure, so the caller must say "I have a DER RSAPrivateKey" or "I have a DER PrivateKeyInfo".

> Design problems aside, I see no reason why it requires this backwards parse.

Yeah, sure. I did not say that supporting this wildcard decode isn't possible with forward parsing. I am just saying we will have to be able to backtrack even to the topmost level.

I think issue-tracking is one of those things where everyone has different preferences, so I won't opine on that, but it sounds like you may be asking whether OpenSSL 3.x's architectural flaws are _the_ cause of the parsing problem. For that, it's hard to say until you try it. It's been a year since I looked into all this for you all, but at least at the time, it was clear that the architectural flaw was the immediate bottleneck. Throughout my idly poking at OpenSSL 3.x, I kept finding inefficient architectural decisions, so I do think focusing on those is the place to start.

Whether it is the _only_ source of the performance regression is hard to say. You'll have to fix the architectural flaw to find out. It may be that the performance will then be on par, or it may be that there's still a regression and a new bottleneck will show up.

I'm absolutely fine with it not being the only problem, my only goal (to speak to your comment on preferences regarding issue tracking), is to identify what we can actually do to mitigate this issue.  That means (to me) identifying a set of concrete tasks that we can execute on to drive this toward closure (which of course will likely involve some profiling/experimentation/iteration/etc).  While github is good for general discussion, Its easy for a long lived issue like this to have the full history of speculation/opinion/general commentary obscure what the goal of the issue is.

So thanks to both you and @beldmit for commenting here, I think if @levitte has some input on the feasibility of the proposal, we can move forward here, and allow subsequent issues to be addressed independently.

Mmm. Sounds like you're trying to navigate a tension between concrete, closable bugs vs not knowing all the 3.0 performance regressions that touch the private key parser. Because of the way 3.0 was developed (a whole slew of far-reaching, risky, and unperformant architectural changes that all landed in one go) as well as how much has been built atop the shaky foundations since, I think that tension is somewhat fundamental. It'll be too difficult to go back and tease apart which architectural decisions impacted performance of which operations. You'll have to instead discover the problems as you fix them.

I dunno how you all like to track bugs, but perhaps then this bug should track the overall performance goal (get 3.0 on par with 1.1.1), and only be closed when you meet that goal. And then you can file child bugs for concrete problems (such as the bad parser architecture) as you identify them, with those being closed as each concrete problem is fixed.

I think you've hit the nail on the head @davidben .  We have a massive slew of issue that amount to "openssl 3.x performance bad" with a rough goal of "openssl 3.0 performance good or better than it was before".  Both are understandable statements, but the issues themselves are typically far reaching, omnibus style bugs that incorporate comments from wide cross sections of the community.  this makes them fairly non-actionable, in terms of being able to say "we're going to fix X in release Y).

As you note, because these issues are largely the result of large architectural changes, its hard to divine all those comments into a set of concrete actions to improve matters.

To that end, we've started from brass tacks in https://github.com/openssl/project/issues/651, running our performance tools to identify specific areas that have regressed from corresponding 1.1.1 code and creating new issues to improve them specifically.  The hope being a long incremental, regimented march toward getting back to where we were.  @alex to your comment about a desire to attain performance metrics simmilar/identical to that of 1.1.1, I don't think I can fairly deliver on that as a goal, because, honestly, its just to big a step to codify in a single issue, or set of issues.

What we can do is what we are doing:
1) Measure 1.1.1 vs 3.x vs master performance for the growing set of tests we have
2) Identify regressions
3) Make incremental fixes to mitigate those regressions
4) goto 1

 In short.  Its not going to be a "fix the performance" effort, its going to be 1000 "fix this little thing and get 1/1000 the performance back" issues.

I'd like to be able to include the information we've captured in issues like these in that effort, but to do so, I need to refine them into a concise statement of what we can do for a given issue, so that the developers (myself included) have a direction to go when making changes.  Without that, I feel as though we are left with a mass of issues that don't identify specific fixes, and performance changes that can't be easily confirmed or refuted, and I need to improve that.

>  @alex to your comment about a desire to attain performance metrics simmilar/identical to that of 1.1.1, I don't think I can fairly deliver on that as a goal, because, honestly, its just to big a step to codify in a single issue, or set of issues.

While saying "OpenSSL 3.x has regressions over 1.1.1" is indeed difficult to evaluate (but still useful as an overall tracking bug), saying "OpenSSL 3.x has regressions over 1.1.1 _for private key parsing_" is a very evaluatable goal because you have a concrete benchmark, or collection of benchmarks.

That's precisely this issue. Like I said, bug organization strategies vary, but if I were organizing fixing all this, I would keep this open as a concrete goal. And then I would have an overall tracking bug linking all the benchmarks I know of where the new release showed a marked performance regression, because even if "OpenSSL 3.x has regressions over 1.1.1" is hard to evaluate, it is a _real problem_. The task from there is to work with the user to help identify the particular operation, so you can graduate to an evaluatable goal.

From there, in investigating these goals, you may identify particular bottlenecks and come up with concrete tasks that will fix things. Those could be one-off PRs if quick and easy, or perhaps an issues tracking those tasks.

> As you note, because these issues are largely the result of large architectural changes, its hard to divine all those comments into a set of concrete actions to improve matters.
>
> In short. Its not going to be a "fix the performance" effort, its going to be 1000 "fix this little thing and get 1/1000 the performance back" issues.

That is not what I'm saying at all. There are certainly a bunch of small mistakes to fix, but when so many problems in a system are caused by architectural changes, it suggests the architecture was bad. In that case, the fix is not fixing 1,000 little things but replacing the bad architecture.

I ran through the start of this exercise for you all a year ago in https://github.com/openssl/openssl/issues/15199#issuecomment-1631038583. I think I'd also pointed out in various other threads how designing a system around format guessing was not only unperformant but also a security risk.

Another example is the provider lookup system and the lazy-loading and global caches. https://github.com/openssl/openssl/discussions/23369 actually came out of me reading through the provider code, because I wanted to see how easy it'd be to build a simpler and more efficient scheme where each provider object is immutable after load. Such a design is much more straightforward to implement correctly and without thread contention. Of course, other architectural flaws will still require you all keep the provider list mutable (and thus perhaps you need the RCU machinery), but there is no good reason for individual providers to be mutable. I would strongly recommend you all think through that, with an eye towards minimizing mutable shared state.

Indeed I think the caches are a symptom of this 1,000 small issues theory. When one sees a single performance issue, it's tempting to add a targeted cache for it, because it's easy and doesn't require rethinking the whole design. And if it is indeed a singular issue, that may even be a good strategy. But when the design itself had problems, the result is caches everywhere. Compounded, this strategy has costs, from a little extra work that every operation needs to do, to thread contention from mutable state, to complexity. They also make benchmarks less representative, as single- and multi-threaded benchmarks no longer translate, and there is amortization hidden behind repeat runs.

Like I said, I would suggest this issue should be "done" when private key parsing, a concrete benchmark, is on par with 1.1.1. That's what OpenSSL's users presumably care about.

From a planning standpoint your concrete tasks here are:
1. Fix the OpenSSL 3.0 architectural flaw identified here
2. Re-evaluate performance
3. If on par, close issue.
4. Else, investigate why you're slower and identify the cause. Goto 1.
@davidben, while I in principle agree with you, I'd say that we can stop pursuing the goal when the 3.x performance is slightly less than 1.1.1 (~10% from the top of my head)
